strengths: Extensive and systematic empirical study spanning multiple datasets (SUN397, Cassava, CIFAR-100 and a 10% subset), two backbone capacities (ViT-Base/ViT-Tiny), and a wide range of privacy budgets and batch sizes/clipping bounds, exposing a clear practical gap in the common practice of fixing (C,B) across settings.

Novel closed-form theoretical result (Theorem 5.1) deriving the MSE-optimal clipping bound as a function of the gradient distribution and noise, offering a plausible mechanistic explanation for why larger C can be better under stronger privacy, contrary to prior asymptotic theory (Koloskova et al.).

The 'clipping as gradient re-weighting' framing and accompanying per-class retained-weight/accuracy analysis (Fig. 4) provide an intuitive and empirically supported explanation of why hard classes suffer disproportionately under aggressive clipping, and this account is used to correctly predict when automatic clipping (AUTO-S) will underperform (validated in Fig. 5).

Careful separation of fixed-steps vs. fixed-epochs regimes for the batch-size analysis, correctly showing that prior sweet-spot heuristics for batch size (Ponomareva et al., Räisä et al.) fail under bounded compute, and proposing an alternative diagnostic based on cumulative DP noise plus a minimum-steps requirement.

Reasonably thorough ablations/appendices (per-model, per-epsilon breakdowns, per-class effects on multiple datasets, effective vs cumulative noise comparisons) that support robustness of the qualitative trends reported in the main text.
weaknesses: All experiments use parameter-efficient fine-tuning (FiLM) with ViT backbones on image classification only; the claim that 'core results... transfer to full-model tuning' and other domains/architectures is asserted but not empirically tested, leaving external validity uncertain.

The batch-size 'rule' in Section 6 is only qualitatively described (combination of a minimum-step threshold and a cumulative-noise plateau) rather than formalized as a precise, validated predictive algorithm; the minimum-step threshold itself is dataset-dependent (e.g., differs between SUN397 and CIFAR-100 per Fig. A14), undermining its use as a general prescription.

Theorem 5.1 minimizes MSE for a single fixed minibatch and ignores multi-step optimization dynamics, momentum/Adam-specific effects, and minibatch sampling noise; while useful for intuition, its connection to final downstream accuracy is argued only qualitatively/via correlation with observed gradient-norm shifts (Fig. 3), not directly validated as a predictor of the empirically optimal C.

No single unified, quantitative rule is proposed that a practitioner could apply out-of-the-box to select C and B jointly for a new task; the contribution is largely diagnostic/explanatory rather than prescriptive, which limits the paper's immediate practical impact despite its clear identification of the problem.

Statistical treatment relies on min-max bands over only 3-5 seeds, and many conclusions are drawn from visual inspection of heatmaps/violin plots rather than formal statistical tests, which is common but leaves some conclusions on the softer/qualitative side (e.g., 'the effect of increasing epochs is more subtle').

strengths: Extensive and systematic empirical study spanning multiple datasets (SUN397, CIFAR-100, Cassava, 20 Newsgroups), multiple backbones (ViT-Tiny, ViT-Base, ResNet-50, DistilBERT), multiple fine-tuning methods (FiLM, LoRA, full fine-tune, from-scratch), and both DP-Adam and DP-SGD optimizers, which is unusually thorough for a hyperparameter study and gives strong empirical support to the core claims.

Identifies and clearly documents a genuine and counterintuitive empirical phenomenon (larger clipping bound helps under stronger privacy/harder tasks) that contradicts common practice and existing heuristics in the DP training literature, which is a valuable contribution to practitioners.

Provides a novel theoretical grounding (MSE decomposition of clipping bias vs. DP noise variance, Theorem 5.2) that is more concrete and interpretable than prior convergence bounds (e.g., Koloskova et al.), and connects it to optimization progress via Theorem 5.4/Corollary 5.5, offering a plausible causal explanation for the empirical observations.

The 'clipping as gradient re-weighting' framing and the per-class retained weight analysis (Fig. 4 and appendix counterparts) provide an intuitive and consistent mechanistic explanation across nearly all experimental settings, strengthening the causal story beyond mere correlation.

The batch-size analysis correctly identifies a real gap in prior heuristics (fixed-steps vs. fixed-epochs regimes) and proposes a reasonably well-motivated alternative (cumulative noise + minimum step count) that is empirically validated across several settings.

Very thorough appendix with extensive additional experiments, ablations (e.g., automatic clipping comparison, full fine-tuning, DP-SGD, LoRA, from-scratch training) that substantially reinforce robustness of the main claims.
Good positioning relative to prior literature, with a clear and balanced related-work discussion showing awareness of contradictory claims in existing work and explicitly aiming to reconcile them.
weaknesses: The theoretical results (Theorem 5.2) explicitly cannot be used prescriptively to select C in practice (as the authors themselves note, since it depends on the actual unknown gradients), so the theory serves mainly as a post-hoc explanatory tool rather than an actionable method; the gap between theory and a deployable clipping-selection algorithm remains.

The proposed batch-size selection rule (cumulative noise plateau + minimum step count) is somewhat heuristic and qualitative (e.g., 'a certain minimum number of steps' varies by dataset, as acknowledged in Fig. A35 caption) rather than a precise, general formula, limiting its immediate practical utility compared to the clean prescriptions in Table 1.

The main text results are predominantly built around the SUN397/ViT-Tiny/ViT-Base combination, with many other settings relegated to the appendix; while appendix evidence is extensive, the paper's central narrative arc could be seen as narrower than the full breadth of experiments suggests.

No explicit discussion of computational cost of the proposed exhaustive grid search (Table A1 grids are large) versus more efficient adaptive or Bayesian hyperparameter search methods used in prior work (e.g., Tobaben et al.), leaving unclear how practical this joint (C,B,η) tuning recommendation is under realistic compute budgets outside of a research setting.

The full fine-tuning result (Section I.3) is somewhat awkwardly integrated as 'the odd one out' and slightly undercuts the generality of the central clipping-difficulty narrative, though the authors do attempt to explain it via gradient norm scale.

Some claims in Table 1 (e.g., 'Lower ε → increase C, decrease B') are presented as general guidance despite the paper itself noting exceptions and caveats (footnote 1, Section 5), creating minor tension between the nuanced empirical findings and the simplified practical takeaways.

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical study spanning multiple datasets (SUN397, CIFAR-100, Cassava, 20 Newsgroups), model backbones (ViT-Tiny/Base, ResNet-50, DistilBERT, WRN-16-4), fine-tuning methods (FiLM, LoRA, full fine-tuning), and optimizers (DP-Adam, DP-SGD), which is unusually comprehensive for this line of work.

Identifies and clearly documents a genuine, practically important discrepancy between prevailing DP-SGD theory/heuristics (smaller C for stronger privacy, larger B is generally better) and empirical behavior, which is a useful contribution to the community given how widespread fixed-hyperparameter practices are.

The gradient re-weighting interpretation of clipping (Eq. 3, Fig. 4) is an intuitive and useful lens that provides a mechanistic, class-level explanation for why clipping bound choice interacts with task difficulty, and it is validated across many additional settings in the appendix.

Derives an exact (not just upper-bounded) MSE-optimal clipping constant under the Gaussian mechanism (Theorem 5.2), which is a modest but non-trivial theoretical addition connecting clipping bias/variance tradeoff and DP noise level explicitly, in contrast to prior bounds (e.g., Koloskova et al.) that depend on unknowable quantities.
The appendix is very extensive with numerous additional experiments, ablations and sanity checks, contributing to reproducibility and thoroughness of the empirical claims.
weaknesses: The theoretical results have limited actionability: the authors explicitly state Theorem 5.2 cannot be used to select C in practice (it requires the true gradients / clipped index set), reducing its role to a post-hoc explanatory device rather than a prescriptive tool, which weakens the practical contribution relative to the paper's framing.
Corollary 5.5 is essentially immediate/trivial (following directly from non-negativity of MSE) and does not add substantive theoretical depth beyond restating Theorem 5.4.

The proposed batch-size selection rule in Section 6 (cumulative noise plus minimum number of steps) is qualitative and heuristic — it is illustrated via visual 'plateau' inspection in figures rather than formalized as an algorithm, and the required minimum number of steps is stated to vary by dataset without a principled way to determine it in advance, undermining its claimed generality.

No quantitative validation of how well the proposed heuristics (Table 1 rules, cumulative-noise batch size rule) predict actual optimal hyperparameters across held-out settings; the paper shows correlational plots but does not report, e.g., prediction accuracy, regret relative to oracle-tuned grid search, or compute savings from using the rule versus full grid search.

Practical guidance remains fairly coarse and qualitative (e.g., 'try larger C', 'avoid large B'), offering limited actionable precision for practitioners compared to the extensive grid search the authors themselves rely on to produce their results.

Central theoretical assumptions (Assumption 5.1: no mini-batch sampling noise; fixed number of clipped gradients in the simplified argument) are quite strong simplifications relative to the actual DP-SGD/Adam training dynamics being explained, raising questions about how tightly the theory really accounts for the empirical phenomena versus serving as a loose post-hoc narrative.

The core empirical finding that clipping bound and batch size should depend on task difficulty is somewhat expected given known bias-variance tradeoffs in the literature (already partially noted by De et al. 2022 and others); the paper's incremental novelty lies mainly in the breadth of empirical demonstration rather than a fundamentally new technique or algorithm.
No mention of code/artifact release, which limits reproducibility of the very large hyperparameter grids and gradient-distribution analyses that underpin the paper's claims.

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical study spanning multiple datasets (SUN397, CIFAR-100, Cassava, 20 Newsgroups), multiple backbones (ViT-Tiny/Base, ResNet-50, DistilBERT, WideResNet), multiple fine-tuning paradigms (FiLM, LoRA, full fine-tuning, training from scratch), and both DP-Adam and DP-SGD, with extensive appendix material supporting the main claims.

Identifies and explains a genuinely counterintuitive and practically important phenomenon: that larger clipping bounds can outperform smaller ones under tighter privacy, contradicting common heuristics/defaults used in prior DP transfer learning literature.

Provides a novel theoretical result (Theorem 5.2) deriving the MSE-optimal clipping bound and connects it to optimization progress (Theorem 5.4, Corollary 5.5), giving a principled explanation for the bias-variance interplay between clipping and DP noise.

The 'clipping as gradient re-weighting' framing and per-class retained-weight analysis (Fig. 4, and many appendix analogues) offers an intuitive and empirically verified mechanism explaining why hard classes/examples are disproportionately harmed by small clipping bounds under difficult learning problems.

Convincingly shows that existing batch-size selection heuristics (based on fixed-steps analyses) fail in the more realistic fixed-epoch/limited-compute setting, and proposes an alternative based on cumulative DP noise plus a minimum-step requirement.
Good related work coverage highlighting genuinely contradictory recommendations in prior literature, motivating the need for this systematic study.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameter grids, dataset descriptions, and experimental settings in the appendix.
weaknesses: Theorem 5.2's optimality result is derived under a simplified assumption (no mini-batch sampling noise, Assumption 5.1) and, as the authors admit, cannot actually be used to select C in practice since it depends on the (privacy-protected) gradients themselves — its role is explanatory rather than prescriptive, limiting the practical impact of the theoretical contribution.

The proposed batch-size selection approach (Section 6) is more of a qualitative heuristic (identify a 'plateau' in cumulative noise plus a minimum-step threshold) than a precise, actionable algorithm; the minimum-step threshold appears to be found empirically/dataset-dependently rather than derived, reducing its generalizability.

Because no efficient/principled way to set (C,B) jointly is proposed beyond exhaustive grid search, the paper's practical recommendation is still costly hyperparameter search — somewhat in tension with the paper's critique of the field's reliance on fixed/limited tuning.

The full-fine-tuning setting (Section I.3) shows a qualitatively different pattern (uniformly large C preferred regardless of difficulty) that partially breaks the clean 'problem difficulty' narrative; while explained post hoc via parameter count/gradient-norm scaling, this is not incorporated into the theoretical framework.

Experiments are restricted to relatively small-to-medium models (up to ViT-Base ~85M params, DistilBERT); it remains unclear how well the findings and heuristics transfer to large-scale LLM DP fine-tuning settings, which is an increasingly important use case.

Statistical robustness is somewhat limited — most results are averaged over only 3-5 seeds, and some plots (e.g., Fig. 5, Fig. A28) show fairly wide min-max bands, raising questions about the significance of some comparisons.

The practical guidance table (Table 1) is fairly coarse/qualitative and offers direction-only advice (increase/decrease) without quantitative guidance on magnitude, limiting its immediate usability by practitioners.
